title: Free grace for all
hook: Arminius and Wesley stressed grace that goes before, freeing everyone to respond

segments.voice: Yesterday, predestination: Reformed Christians resting in God's choosing, a hand that won't let go. Your line was held by his choosing. What did you loosen your grip on? Day one thousand seventy-nine.

"The God of my mercy shall prevent me." That's a psalm, in the King James Bible, and to a modern ear it sounds alarming. Prevent me? Stop me? But in the English of that Bible, to prevent could mean to come before, to go ahead of. The psalm is saying God's mercy will go out in front. Keep that old meaning in your pocket, because a family of churches uses it for one of their teachings. John Wesley, the Methodist leader, liked to call it preventing grace. Today it usually goes by a longer Latin-flavored word. Today: prevenient grace.
screen: `THE GOD OF MY MERCY SHALL PREVENT ME.`

segments.voice: Prevenient grace: grace that comes before. Yesterday the Reformed said God chooses first, and salvation rests on that choosing. Jacob Arminius, a Dutch teacher, and later John Wesley in England, agreed on the first part: grace must come first. Nobody climbs to God by their own strength. Augustine was right about that, they said. But they read the Bible's wide words widely. John's Gospel calls Christ "the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world." Every man. Titus says: "the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men." And Jesus says, in John: "And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me." So, they taught, God's grace goes ahead of everyone, not only some. It wakes the conscience. It loosens the bent will just enough that a person can say yes to God, or turn away. Wesley spoke of it as the first faint wish to please God, the first dawn of light. The yes still matters. But even the yes is a gift. Methodists and other Wesleyan and Holiness churches stand in this line, and so do some Pentecostals. The Reformed reply that it gives too much weight to the human choice. Wesleyans reply that love leaves room for a real answer, yes or no. Both sides quote scripture, both say grace first, and both pray. The first letter of John has a line both could sign: "We love him, because he first loved us." The disagreement is over what happens next.
screen: `WE LOVE HIM, BECAUSE HE FIRST LOVED US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: respond to one nudge of good. Settle, and breathe. Then wait, and listen inward. Maybe there's a small nudge you've been stepping around: text that person, apologize for that thing, give that coat away, call an old friend. Don't invent one. Just notice the one that's already there. Let it get clear. Then decide on one small step you'll take today to answer it. If you pray, you can give thanks for the nudge itself. If you don't, simply notice that the nudge came before you chose to listen. The bell holds the time.
Prevenient grace. Grace that goes before anyone chooses, reaching everyone and freeing them to answer. Arminius and Wesley stressed it.
Your line: grace goes before. Today, take the one small step you chose, before the nudge fades. Day one thousand seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Methodist and other Wesleyan churches teach prevenient grace, God's grace going before every person and enabling them to respond, and their hymns and preaching often invite people to answer that grace.

fork.setup: you're John Wesley. you agree with Augustine that grace must come first. but John's Gospel says the light lighteth every man. what do you teach?
options: grace comes only to a chosen few.
grace goes before everyone, freeing each person to answer.

fork.reveal: Wesley taught preventing grace: God's grace goes ahead of everyone, waking the conscience and freeing the will to say yes, or to turn away.

notes: 'In the English of that Bible, to prevent could mean to come before': the KJV itself shows the sense (Psalm 59:10; 1 Thessalonians 4:15). Confirm the wording.
Wesley's 'preventing grace' and 'the first wish to please God, the first dawn of light' are paraphrased from Sermon 85 (On Working Out Our Own Salvation); confirm the sermon number and section.
'Methodists and other Wesleyan and Holiness churches stand in this line, and so do some Pentecostals': confirm. 'Jacob Arminius, a Dutch teacher' and 'John Wesley, the Methodist leader': confirm.
The Reformed and Wesleyan replies are given in parallel without ranking. Confirm both sides would recognize themselves.
Original-language game left null: there is no single biblical word for prevenient grace (the Latin gratia praeveniens is a later theological term).
Editor: hook no longer says churches 'built a teaching on' the psalm's word; practice no longer tells the listener a nudge is probably there.
Auditor: 'love which can't be refused isn't love' read as a jab at the Reformed view of God's love; softened to a positive statement of the Wesleyan concern.
